utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dosenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to remind you again that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Do you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My paper. My book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's your report --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in hard copy. Mr. McCloskey, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, every one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning sir, to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how are you this morning?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just want to go back briefly to what's been MFI'd as P7503. And, sir, that -- you'll remember from yesterday that we showed you a document and there was some discussion on whether or not it was a teletype and whether it had the complete order on it or not. And we had the original of that, that we received from the Drina Corps collection which I'd like you to take a look at. I had a chance to go over that a bit with Mr. Ivetic this morning. But there's the first page of the document and we might as well go to the last page. I think we'll recall that that was the part that there was some things that appeared to be missing from the other document, the signed version of this, if everyone remembers. And I think if you look at the last part of that, you can see that it looks like the keys have typed away for the last couple of lines, but for some reason it doesn't look like there was ink on it. Is that what it looks like to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to the page 3 of this document so that -- we can see what we're talking about on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, for the record, it was yesterday at page transcripts 37882 that you thought that this was a typewriter. In any event now that you've had a chance to look at that, what's your view? Is this a teletype?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still maintain that this is typewritten and it seems the tape had run out or was -- or has faded, the ribbon has faded. And it says Milovanovic in the signature, and it was transmitted via communications that it was SR, which means signed personally, so there must be a handwritten document somewhere in the archives. I cannot say anything about the content because that's not my area of competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. On that point, you remember you rightfully pointed out us that the first document I showed you had a signature on it and, therefore, would not have been sent over the teletype. So that's the original you were speaking of; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot relate these two documents in any way. I would have had to have both of them in front of me to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'm not sure we need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, are you at all interested in seeing the original?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it's good to see it. You mean the original of this one? Yes, I'd like to have a look at it. And could the witness explain why he is convinced that it's typewritten and not teleprinted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Teletype machines do not use ribbons, the modern ones used in the VRS; and typewriters do use a ribbon. That's the difference. And based on that, I see that this was typewritten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I put the following to you: If a typist sees that what he types doesn't appear due to a lack of a ribbon or whatever, would that person using a typewriter, would they continue for lines and lines to type without anything appearing on paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm convinced that the operator of the teletype, when receiving, would have noticed it and then he would have replaced the ribbon, so I don't understand, regardless of whether it was a telegraph -- a typewriter or a teletype. I have no explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And how do you explain that this piece of paper bears an original stamp with some handwritten entries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that lends a very strange aspect to this document. And the person placing the stamp would -- should be the chief of -- the chief of clerks or somebody like that. It's strange that this stamp is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the stamp indicate, as far as you're concerned, that this message was sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a received document. So, de facto, according to the stamp, it was received. You see the initials of the person who signed for the receipt. We could probably find that person based on the initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now is it your position interpreting that someone received this text and typed that out and that it was not more or less automatically put on paper by a machine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot give you any comment. Both the operator and the chief of clerks would notice that something is not right with this document. I have -- I cannot explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Only one question in addition to that. You said it was received, that is what we can see from the stamp; that's correct. Received by whom? Was it on the sender or receiver side of the transmitter system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's obvious that this is on the part of the receiving party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What makes you certain about that assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not my assumption. I see it on the stamp. It says "received," and logically that means that it was done or stamped by the receiving party and there should be the stamp, the signature we here should be the signature of the person who received it. We see "Manojlo Milovanovic," but there is no rank. We don't see an indication of whether he signed it or not. So the fact is that this is on the side of the receiving party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What makes you believe that's no rank in the badly legible part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither below nor above the lettering where we see "OJLO" - because the beginning of that word is punched through - there is no trace that anything else was omitted as the other few lines were omitted. Maybe the tape -- the ribbon had completely run out. But how could that be if it managed to type Manojlo Milovanovic and not the rest of the lines if they had been present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties are invited to look at the original, whether the word "Potpukovnik" ^ is appearing. That's one. Second -- now, if something is typewritten and it runs out of ribbon, when restarting or when typing legible text again, you would start where it became illegible and do it again, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the operator should notice that the ribbon is not useable anymore and if he were a professional at typing, looking at the text, he would not be looking at the machine and the paper he is typing on. That could be an explanation. And if he then saw there was no writing and then changed something to the signature, that, I could find no explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A person typing a text would resume at the spot where the ink is running out and therefore complete the text; whereas, a machine can't resume, can't repeat what is done already. Would you agree with that or would you have any comment on what I just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If he should notice that he could go back to the line that was not well typed, if it were a person, but, still, you would -- it would be noticeable that the operator had gone back on the typewriter. But just more likely is the scenario that he would take the whole paper out and re-type the whole thing again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But a machine couldn't type down again what was lost meanwhile, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, electrical typewriters could not do that. At least I haven't seen electrical typewriters with a memory. If they existed, I know that they were not used at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My -- you may have misunderstood my question. I compared a person typing a text with a tele-writing machine, which receives signals and puts it on text. Once a portion is lost there, the machine can't go back and repeat what is missing, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a machine cannot do that alone. However, teletype machines also have a ribbon that goes along with the paper and it's perforated and if something is amiss, it turns the perforated ribbon or tape back and re-types what was missing; whereas, a machine cannot do that alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please proceed. The original will be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you know, and -- does a -- the teletype machine used by the VRS have an ink ribbon or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Teletype machines used by the Army of Republika Srpska did not have ribbons. Some old teleprinters received a long time back from the US had them, but those were obsolete even then. They were not in use, especially none with this font.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're the chief of communications, you would have seen the teletype machines and the teletype paper. Do you remember the name of one of the machines that was in common use at the time as an ETL-1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said -- yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, sir, maybe you'll remember that and this court has heard with Mr. Jevdjevic, as a matter of fact, who went over several teletyped intercepts and the Court has seen a very unique narrow printer that comes out of a teletype, an ETL-1. There's another printer that the Drina Corps had that they went over with Jevdjevic and it was a bit wider. And they've also seen typed documents from the Rogatica Brigade which was regular typing size paper, A4. So, and we don't need to worry too much about this, but just think back, this is the narrow teletype printer from an ETL and an ETL that uses ribbon, as I'm showing you in my right hand, that we just pulled out of our ETL upstairs. So just think back. This -- this is a teleprinter; right? This is a teleprinter document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that it's from a teleprinter, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is a teleprinter ribbon, 160 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was a different one. Do you allow that the original you just had in your hands comes from a teleprinter, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just for the record we have an image of the ribbon that we'll -- so we can have the record clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another topic, the last topic we mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the document was MFI'd. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it was MFI'd because of the issues yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was MFI'd because of a lack of a translation, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, yes, and we were going to work out the last part so I guess we need to get it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that having looked now at the original that the party also be able or find someone a technician who is able to also reproduce the text where apparently the ink is missing but where the imprint is pretty clear could be reproduced so as to compare the whole of the document with the other version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, we have a person that is very good at that, who will be back soon and we'll get that sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Last topic. You remember I asked you a bit about Ljubisa Beara yesterday and you answered you knew who he was. And I want to take you back to 1994 and 1995. I know that's a long time to remember, but do you remember Ljubisa Beara sending out a document that went to your corps where he was rather concerned about the sloppy radio communications over the air, and also attached to that document an intercepted conversation that his -- that the -- that the Intel Department of The VRS had actually intercepted from VRS communications and he used it as an example of what not to do. Do you remember that rather unique situation?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't remember. Maybe it reached the corps command, but I was often on field missions in the so-called IKMs, forward command posts of brigades at the foremost front line, spending a few days there on each stint. I -- I don't think I've seen it. I just don't remember such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I correct myself. It was actually sent to the security Department of Your -- of the 2nd Krajina Corps, so you may have heard it from your own security officer.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the chief has a department for intelligence and security and then he has an assistant chief for security and another assistant chief for intelligence. So I don't know which one was involved here. And they usually do not present documents that they receive to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at 65 ter 25184, and that's the document that Naval Captain or Colonel, as we know, Ljubisa Beara sent out to the security units, the corps. And I won't read it all, but as we -- wait until that English comes up. We'll see that it's from the Main Staff. And let's just flip over to the second page in English so we can confirm that I've got my people right. Yeah, there's Naval Captain Beara. Okay, so let's go back to the first page, and let's see the bottom of the Serbian so that we can see... sorry. We must need to go to the second -- the second page of the Serbian. Yeah, there's Mr. Beara. Okay. So going back to the first page of the Serbian. And we see that just in that first paragraph, he says: "As everyone is aware and since the Main Staff ... and lower commands have point the out many times, military secrets are constantly being leaked via communications equipment (radio relay devices and radio stations)." Then he talks about operations to take away some of these smaller radios that were a problem. And then he talks about, in the third paragraph, that they've learned from electric -- excuse me, electronic reconnaissance. And this is a -- he's referring to a VRS communication here, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Electronic surveillance by the enemy vis-à-vis the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, he says here in the last sentence: "We have learned only by accident about the negligence in the use of our communications." Then he says: "Here is the latest example of careless use of communications equipment." And then he gives a segment - and we can go to the next page in English - of a conversation on the 29th of August between a certain Djukic from the Ozren Tactical Group to his superior and it's mentioning Kelecevic. Do you know who a Kelecevic was perhaps from the Ozren Tactical Group or from Doboj, the --

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know many Kelecevics in war. I know that the Chief of Staff of the 1st Krajina Corps was a Kelecevic. Now whether he is the person meant here or some other Kelecevic, I cannot tell on the basis of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, where can I find the name Kelecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we have to go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we see here what -- what Colonel Beara is -- is doing, and if we try to remember a bit about this conversation, I want to show you now 65 ter 32091. And, sir, what you're seeing here is a handwritten notebook of intercept operations of a group of Bosnian army intercept operators from an area called Tesanj. And this is -- I have another document that shows that this is it from August 29th, and we see that it's at 1145 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: August 29th of what year, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- well, the time is slightly different than the other one that I said. If we look at this, we see that Kelecevic is mentioned. And if we go to the next page, and if we compare the intercepts in the Beara document and the text on this intercept minus the part that is in brackets here, which is apparently another conversation that came in between the main one, we'll see that it's the same conversation. And if we go back to the front page of this document, we see that it's 762. And that would be a reference to the frequency of a RRU-800; correct? We need the first page of the -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got the right page in front of me where the second -- the lower part of the page is the Arsic-Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As the president said, take a look at the lower part of the page you'll see the Arsic-Djukic intercept we're talking about. And you'll see it says 762 and then in (80). And my question is that reference in 762 (80), that's a reference to the frequency; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't see that this pertains to a frequency at all. I believe that, rather, this has to do with some kind of numbers documents. 762 megahertz, it is a frequency or, rather, it is -- I mean, well, on a RRU-800 but not 80, even not with single channel equipment, so I cannot link this to that. I believe that this has to do with some kind of numbering of theirs as regards the writing of these documents, taking notes et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would have you an explanation as why, then, all the documents on this page all bear the same number? Which may be confusing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably this could be deciphered if we look at the next note and see whether that's that numbering or not. However, regardless of everything, I'm convinced that it has nothing to do with frequency because 762 and 80 cannot be linked up at all. 762 megahertz, that's a RRU-800 and as for 80 megahertz that's not a single piece of equipment in the VRS that operated using that. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any chance that 8-0 stands for the 800? The RRU-800.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. It would have said 8, as was customary, for RRU-800s, or it would have said 800, but it wouldn't have been only 80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you familiar with -- with the way in which they jotted down this by the other armed forces? Or is it just speculation that you say, We would do it differently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a rule on station diaries --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where it says where, at what time, and at which frequency somebody received something so it's not particularly coded. It's all written down. So there are regulations. If they deviated from that, then one could not say anything here that it's a frequency or some kind of internal numbering of their own or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 32890. Should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, as you will be able to see that this is a document from the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the 2nd Corps, dated 26 August 1995. And in that first paragraph it notes: "The following information on radio relay links of the aggressor relating to the Ozren Tactical Group and the Doboj Operation Group has been obtained: The quality of the signal and the traffic on the said frequencies has been checked and a special report will be sent on this." And if we look down and we get to the section or multi-channel RRU, we see that 762.100 says Ozren and Doboj. So that would indicate that 762 in the previous intercept was actually 762 is the first three digits of a RRU-800 frequency; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this column everything is RRU-800 and FM-200 and the other one up there is RRU-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the 762, that's the same number we saw on the notebook regarding the intercept that we just looked at; correct? An intercept that happened to be between the Ozren Tactical Group and ...?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this can, quite simply, overlap. This numbering of theirs with some kind of frequency or whatever else. So I cannot accept that this is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to 65 ter 32889. And this is just the page in the notebook that indicates the date of 29 August 1995 that I'm sure we'll all agree is on the front of this, helping us with the date. It's page 40. That's the first page of the notebook that we have on the screen now. But we should go to page 40 in e-court for the date. There we see it. All right. And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So at this point, Mr. President, I would offer the document from Colonel Beara, which was 65 ter 25184 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25184 receives exhibit number P7504, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And also if I could have the Muslim army intercept which was -- we saw that is 65 ter 32091.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the -- just the pages you referred to or is it the whole of that book?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The whole -- the -- that 65 ter is just three pages so that's just the intercept, according to Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 32091 receives exhibit number P7505, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the document that we saw that noted the frequencies, another document from the BiH command and that was 65 ter 32890.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P7506.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7506 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be 7506. Now it's correct on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that I said that it was admitted under seal, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And lastly, just that one page with the 29 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, do we need -- Mr. Ivetic, is there any dispute as to what we looked at in this book that that follows the 29th of 8, that's 29th of August, is the last entry for the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If that's what we have on our screen, that's what we have on our screen. I have not looked at the entire notebook to say anything beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we hear from you whether there's any dispute whether what was admitted into evidence follows immediately by this date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. In that case I won't offer that last one -- well, the one with the date on it, of course, is -- I just noticed is the entire notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. The one with the date on is the entire notebook and I think the entire notebook -- could the parties after the break inform the Chamber whether there's any dispute as to the entries we looked at are following an indication of the date being the 29th of August, 1995. We'd like to hear from you after the break. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, lastly, Witness, along with that, that packet of material that we just showed you that we got from the BiH army, they provided us an audiotape that contained this intercept, and I recall you testifying about whether or not the ABiH could hear both sides of a duplex conversation, and I would like us to listen to some of this conversation which, in the Prosecution's position, is a duplex conversation, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which one is it? Is it with the Drina Corps or with some other unit? Are we going beyond?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would love to take the witness-stand but I'm sorry, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This intercept. I do understand the intercept that we looked at 29th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one we looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Same subject, same intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he's referring to the witness as saying whether or not the ABiH could hear both sides of a duplex conversation, which was in relation to the Drina Corps as I recall and the set-ups of the two listening posts so ... I'm wondering if we're going beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the Defence agrees that other units of the ABiH could listen to both sides of the conversation, I may not need to play this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm focussing on the units that are being listened to, not who is doing the listening. Let him play the tapes and let him ask the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that's the best way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the tape is about five minutes, which we don't need five minutes of. I think Ms. Stewart informs me she can play about the last one minute and there is no transcript but we're just listening to try to -- see if we can distinguish the parties and the way they're speaking to each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And have -- has the transcript -- there's no transcript at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're then just listening to voices, to sound, rather than to text at this moment and we don't expect - because our interpreters are usually not in a position to interpret immediately something they have not been prepared for. So, therefore, let's see whether it makes any sense to listen to it by listening to the last minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And should we move to the B/C/S channel in order to follow it, Mr. McCloskey? How is it organised?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We should be fine on our regular channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we hear the B/C/S on the English channel as well, without interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And we start at 3 minutes and 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, as -- just so you know that the end of that intercepted conversation and then the -- it's the Prosecution's position that the tape continued to record and we heard that last part. Can you -- as -- tell us, was that the sounds of some telephone or some piece of equipment ringing and being picked up when the person said, Allo?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as regards audibility perhaps I'm an elderly man and I cannot hear very well but others have been listening to and can judge it. I barely understood anything. At the very end, you see that somebody is automatically dialling a telephone, an automatic telephone, and on the other end there is a micro telephone conversation and this person is answering the phone and saying hello. I really cannot conclude anything whether it is two channels, one channel, cable, and so on. It could have happened in every conceivable way so this does not show in any way that it was a duplex. Secondly, if a duplex communication is being intercepted, you can never hear both participants in the same way. I already spoke about electromagnetic waves and how they go through the atmosphere. It's not always the same. It's different. So automatically the tones are going to be different. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I put the following to you. When listening to the first part of the conversation I heard sometimes someone speaking very clearly and sometimes, then, part of the conversation was where I heard a voice which was with a lot of rumble around it, less audible, which gave me the impression - but I'm not drawing any conclusions - that the one person, which I could clearly hear, was one of the interlocutors whereas the rumbled voice was the other one so that I gained the impression that I was listening to the both sides of the conversation. That is my personal impression. Do you have any comment on this impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is something here called strong fading so I would not say that the other one was not a wire communication. The other one was a wire communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? "The other one was a wire communication."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, because what could be heard was the dialling of a dial on an automatic telephone. So it wasn't that somebody was pressing buttons, but, rather dialling. Secondly, it rang a few times and that could be heard quite clearly and when the other person said hello that was heard quite clearly. There wasn't this fading effect, this noise. That appears only in wireless communication, not in wire communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was about the first portion I listened to, and you apparently are commenting on the last portion on which I did not give any impression. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was my question, which he answered it the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I have nothing further, Mr. President. Though I would offer this portion -- well, the full five minutes of that tape, four-plus minutes of that tape into evidence and we will provide a transcript and perhaps we will be able to distinguish, for someone listening to the tape and looking at the transcript, where we think the people changed, so you can, when hearing, you can see if there's two people or not. But no new evidence, just perhaps an exhibit that will help the non-Serbian speaker sort it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then it should be MFI'd until we get that transcript and make further submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think, as a matter of fact, the audio in itself, that is just the sound not interpreted in terms of text, that's what we listened to. That gives the Chamber an opportunity to have observed personally by listening what it heard. Now, if anything to further clarify that is text, et cetera, would be added, I would agree with you, Mr. Ivetic, that we can't decide on that at this moment. We can, however, decide on just the audiotape as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you heard the whole thing. But you only heard one segment and he is offering five minutes. So I think we still have to see what's the rest of that to see whether it's something. I mean, we don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- could you just limit it to the portion we heard, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would prefer in that case to play the whole thing. It's an important topic, we spent God knows how many days on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you can't off the part that we listened to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure technically we could. But it was pretty short. You get a better feel for it when you hear the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Since ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll listen to after the break. Witness, we'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you give us an impression as to how much time you would need in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think about half an hour, give or take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take the break and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait, Your Honours, in relation to the big book that we saw and the date of 29 August, 1995, the excerpt that has been admitted as P07505 does come after the date. If that's what Your Honours had asked before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, with no other dates in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record. Mr. Dosenovic, we're going to listen to the entirety of the intercept you have listened to before. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If Ms. Stewart could start that from the beginning and if we recall it was 32888a. Than -- when I say "the beginning," that should be the beginning of the four minutes we just heard the last-within-a-minute part. So this will be more, starting from the beginning of the tape we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, that would conclude the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now you are tendering the entire ... are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, any objections to the tendering of the audiotape without having, at this moment, a text, just to enable the Judges to personally observe or hear what -- that there is a kind of a conversation and whether both interlocutors can be heard. Because that's -- Mr. McCloskey, I understood, is the main purpose of this -- of this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, it's relating to a different area, but I'll get that in the cross -- in the re-direct. But I think we still need that marked for identification pending a translation to follow the correct procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact we're not supposed to listen to text at this moment. Again, if that is added at a later point in time then, of course, we would need translation. It's just to get an audio impression of a conversation, the content, whether it's the same or not, if Mr. McCloskey wants to argue that it's the same as one of the -- one of the -- it's not the one of the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This audiotape reflects the intercept that upset Mr. Beara and that the Muslim army received --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- the text of. So we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's clear then. If you want to argue -- I mean, at this moment, I think we are at a point where the Chamber can hear whether the full conversation of this intercept can be heard, yes or no. What it is, you say it's the same. The Chamber doesn't know. The Chamber can't establish that. So the probative value is limited to hearing a conversation. And if you want to draw conclusions that go further and apparently you are, then have you to provide the Chamber with further information about this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President. And the primary purpose as I said before was so that you could listen to both sides of a conversation, which is the Prosecution's position is a duplex conversation. It also goes to the authenticity of the intercept that we saw, which is the -- not only as we now heard by the VRS but by the BiH. So it's primarily one purpose but I don't want you to exclude it for the other purposes as well. And I think you're best off with the transcript so you can make that connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you say it's a duplex then you link it to some document in which it is mentioned or suggested that this was a duplex conversation. Of course, the only thing we know is that you can hear both parties and what kind of a connection it was from this document itself, we can't draw any conclusions. Now I leave it up to you, if you want, for the very limited purposes, tender it, and then we would admit it on that basis, or would you rather first prepare a transcription so that we can link the content to any other exhibit you may want to -- that is in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The latter, I think it's a good idea that we link it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we mark it for identification for the time being, awaiting further submissions, especially transcription and translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 32888a receives exhibit number P7507, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed -- no, "please proceed," I should say this to Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Dosenovic, you'll now further be examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You were asked about reflection of transmissions from bouncing off of mountains at transcript page 37840 and onwards. I'd like to take a look at - but it should not be broadcast - 1D5847 with you. And, first of all, on this first page, we see that the southern location is number 1 and the northern location is number 2? If we can now turn to page 14 of this document, also not broadcasting the same. And if we could perhaps zoom in to the actual diagram. Sir, first of all, have you seen this particular diagram previously?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen it, sir. I had it in my possession. From this, you can see Vlasenica is 120 metres, at 120 metres distance, the first obstacle is at 885 metres, as far as I can see -- no, no, no. 120 metres is Vlasenica. The first obstacle is at around 885 metres, which means the difference in altitude is 50 or 60 metres, and I told the Prosecutor that if there is a feature in Vlasenica higher than 50 metres, then you could place a work station there for intercepting, and the Prosecutor himself said that Major Jevdjevic said exactly in which building it was in the centre of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- could you please, Mr. Ivetic, the question is whether the witness has seen this particular diagram so he apparently has. That was a yes or no question. Now the witness immediately went on 120 metres. I don't see 120 metres anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's what I was going do ask next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore you should have intervened right at the beginning and take the lead and put specific questions. That's the reason why I intervened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The B/C/S was one thing and the English was another that is what I was trying to do without directing it, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Witness, the English translation said that the Vlasenica at 120 metres. Could you please comment on that. Is that accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where does the English say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have a hard copy of it that is much easier to read than the screen. It might help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with giving him a hard copy. But I believe that he actually said something different because I do have one ear off on my headset and can listen to the Serb that is spoken. But if we want to give him a hard copy, that's fine. I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, if you want to give it to the witness, that's fine. With the help of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have the map, but it's -- it's -- from a different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... location than the one he's got. If you remember, it comes from different places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have no hard copy of this very document, then we'll just proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask you just to repeat ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you to repeat for us what you said the elevation of Vlasenica was that you could see from this diagram.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said Vlasenica is at 820 metres. The first obstacle closest towards the southern station was --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the rest we have. The question I have is in relation to the Prosecution's questions about bouncing off -- transmissions off of mountains, given the placement of the obstacles that you've identified that are closer to Vlasenica and further away from the southern listening post, could such transmissions be bounced off of those mountains or not, in the manner that the Prosecution has indicated during their cross?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The obstacle is such that electromagnetic waves cannot pass in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if the parabolic antenna of the ABiH at the southern post was intended to capture signals bouncing from obstacles on the ground, what kind of angle would you expect that parabolic antenna to be set at?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic thing is that electromagnetic waves just as the light reflects at an angle of 95 degrees so if the mask is in front and even if they bounce off and can be received, they could only be received at a place opposite of the receiving station at the southern installation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now we see this diagram is a curved type. Could you please explain for us what that curvature indicates.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a complete diagram for the verification of radio visibility in the first bottom curvature in the middle is marked with zero. The middle, between two posts that should have communication. The next one is above 5 kilometres to the left and 5 kilometres to the right. The next full line is 10 kilometres to the left, 10 kilometres to the right. That means the points connected with this curvature are on the same plane. That's the essence of this diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your cross-examination, you mention that you checked certain optical visibility points to confirm whether there was or was not a line of sight and you used string. Could you please explain for us on what you would use string to perform the type of test that you said you performed.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a topographic map of any scale and for such calculations you must usually take 1 to 100.000 and a ruler and simply on a map you draw a line between these two points, using a ruler, and you see if there is an obstacle. In front of them you cannot place radio relay communication there. If there is something interfering, then you see in the manual for signalsmen, which is like a Bible to them, you can find a suitable place more easily than on a map. It's very simple, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to clarify, you said "if there's something interfering on the topographic map, then you see in the manual for signalsmen, which is a like a Bible to them you can find a suitable place." What is the next step, according to the manual? What is then done to determine optical visibility for the purposes of setting up radio stations?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place that I selected for a station has to be higher than all the obstacles in the way. It has to be at the same altitude or higher. If an obstacle appears, then have you to move the station, place it somewhere else. And we always take care that a -- the beam doesn't go towards the enemy; or, if it does, that it should be lateral.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how does a diagram like this one relate to the manual for signalsmen?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it coincides because there is the so-called Fresnel zone so if the obstacle is somewhere close to the line I drew on the map, then I take that manual and I see whether at least the first Fresnel zone passes through that feature to -- to calculate radio visible and the Fresnel zone is the zone through which the highest energy of the electromagnetic waves go from one station to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 19 - again not broadcast - this should be the northern facility with Vlasenica again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ivetic, could we first focus on what we see on our screen now and to understand what exactly is depicted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we're back on that page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could enlarge it slightly. There's no translation of this document, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't have one, although it's -- the Prosecution has a 65 ter number of a similar document just without the numbers 1 and 2 with the actual names. I don't know if that one has a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But for this one, at this moment, there's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, did you yourself make this diagram? Could you answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said Vlasenica was at 820 metres altitude. Do you have an explanation as why it is on this diagram that Vlasenica is put at a little bit over 500 metres rather than a little bit over 800 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's the place, and that's its altitude, if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's plotted on the diagram which apparently has vertically the altitude of points to be connected, then I would have expected 820 metres, Vlasenica, a little bit higher up. Do you have any explanation for it being somewhere in the range of the low 600s rather than on the 800s?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately, I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I see that various positions, I do understand the -- one is the radio relay station, the intercept, is at 1326 metres, and I find that plotted on this diagram just above the 1300-metres mark, which I understand. However, for the Vlasenica altitude, I find it plotted on this diagram close to the 600 line rather than close to the 800 line. Do you have any explanation for that? Perhaps the usher could assist by moving -- perhaps the usher could assist by moving the cursor at the 600 line and slowly going in the direction of where it is written "Vlasenica." Now I see there are 600 line and I see 820 metres. Any explanation for plotting one altitude in accordance with the numbers and the other one quite different from what I see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this diagram is not correct. It's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But -- okay. Now have I another -- in that respect, apparently it's not correct. Mr. McCloskey, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have -- I can resolve this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can resolve it. Okay. I give you an opportunity to do that very soon. You said there were two obstacles. Which are these obstacles? Could you describe what they are? And so not -- not how they were plotted on this diagram but what are they? Are they buildings; and if so, what building? Is it anything else? Is it a hill? Is it -- what are the obstacles that are plotted on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the obstacles that are plotted there are hills, mountains. So it is land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But which hill is the one and which hill is then the other, if these are hill as soon as.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that cannot be seen in this diagram. It can be seen in a map though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you know what these obstacles - because you talked about them - what they are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Topographically speaking everything above 500 metres is a mountain. So they are mountains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they're not buildings. You know that for sure. Because buildings could be an obstacle as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They can, Your Honour. But here it is marked down here that the first obstacle is 2 and a half kilometres away from the station and the second one is 3.9 kilometres away. So at that distance a building would not constitute a problem, even if it were quite tall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is on a mountain, that building? Usually buildings are not built at sea level but they are usually constructed in the landscape. If there are hills, you build a building on a hill. Would that make any difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it would be taken into account if it was higher than 20 metres. But in view of the width of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, but what I want to know is: Do you know what hill it is, whether it is accounted for there is a building on it? Which are these hills?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know just off the cuff. I'd need to see a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you don't have the knowledge apparently. You say -- if you say, I have to see a map, you are reconstructing what, in your view, most likely would be the obstacle, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am sure that it is the land itself. The building -- or a building could not constitute a problem in view of the width of the magnetic beam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's understood. But you don't know what these obstacles, what hills are presented on this diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic. We now at least know what we are looking at. But Mr. McCloskey offered his assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's a significant problem that we need to clear up to for this to go on. It's not a big problem. It's to the benefit for everyone. If we could ask -- the witness needs not to be here when I offer this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or you would rather have him not here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That would be a better way of saying it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because. Witness, would you follow the usher for a second to leave the courtroom because Mr. McCloskey would tell us something which we would like not you to bother with at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We -- this diagram comes from Mr. Rodic's annex. We have a good copy of it. Our copy shows that Vlasenica is at 620 metres, as -- which would make it consistent with the map as you've indicated. They're looking at a -- a copy, as we can see that it looks like 8. And I don't know -- you know, I'm not suggesting that anything has been fiddled with. I think it's just a bad reproduction. When you're determining optical sight, of course that's significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MILE DOSENOVIC [Resumed]
